newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac launches reform of French justice.
newsitem.headline: Chirac launches reform of French justice.

text.p: President Jacques Chirac, keen to distract attention from record unemployment and corruption scandals, launched a major reform of France's justice system on Monday, calling for greater independence for the judiciary, and better protection of the right to be presumed innocent.
In a television address, Chirac said: "Suspicions remain about the independence of magistrates from the political authorities. Fundamental human rights are sometimes ignored.

"The time has come to set a great ambition for our justice system: refounding the principles on which it is based, modernising its methods and adapting them to our times. I want to achieve this great reform in my seven-year term," he said.

Chirac said a 21-member bipartisan commission headed by Supreme Court president Pierre Truche would report by July 15 on ways of guaranteeing judicial independence, an alternative source of legitimacy for the judiciary and improving respect for the presumption of innocence.

"It will examine how the independence of the judicial branch can be increased by changing or abolishing the hierarchical link which currently ties the public prosecutor to the justice minister," Chirac said. He said the government would offer legislation to parliament after receiving the report.

He did not mention allegations that his government had tried to obstruct a wave of investigations into alleged illicit funding of his Gaullist party by rake-offs from public works contracts while he was mayor of Paris between 1977 and 1995.
Dozens of businessmen and fundraisers, including former RPR personnel chief Louise-Yvonne Casetta, have been placed under judicial investigation but none has yet been brought to trial.

Chirac said France's courts were choking with an overload of cases, denying citizens timely recourse to justice. He asked the government to present in July a five-year plan to simplify litigation procedures, make greater use of conciliation and mediation, and increase spending on the justice system.
He compared the importance of the reform with last year's overhaul of the armed forces with the abolition of conscription and a controversial reform of the welfare system.

The commission announced by the Justice Ministry included the chairman of the Agence France-Presse news agency, Jean Miot, the editor of Roman Catholic daily La Croix, Noel Copin, philosophers Blandine Barret-Kriegel and Luc Ferry, Supreme Court prosecutor Jean-Francois Burgelin and a former aide to the late president Francois Mitterrand, Jean Kahn.

Political analysts said Chirac's initiative had the dual advantage of countering criticism over the corruption probes and diverting national debate from economic stagnation, unemployment, deficit-cutting and the single European currency.

Since the government could not enact an amnesty for party funding offences, which proved politically disastrous for its Socialist predecessors in 1990, it could at least show it was doing its best to clean up the justice system.
However, some conservative politicians have expressed doubts about making the judiciary fully independent.

Parliamentary legal committee chairman Pierre Mazeaud warned of a "government of judges" and questioned who would set penal policy if prosecutors and magistrates were not appointed by elected political authorities.

Jean-Marie le Pen, leader of the extreme-right National Front, said he was not convinced judges were more trustworthy than politicians. "At least we can judge politicians through elections. How could we judge the magistrates and where would their legitimacy come from?" he asked.

The Higher Magistrates' Council, which recommends senior judicial appointments to the president, submitted a memorandum to Chirac last week suggesting two relatively simple measures would be sufficient to guarantee judicial independence.

It said the justice ministry should no longer appoint or promote prosecutors and magistrates, whose careers would be managed by the independent council, and the minister should be barred from giving orders to prosecutors in individual cases.
Opposition Socialist party spokesman Francois Hollande said there was no need for the Truche commission since the president only needed to follow the council's advice.
